title: Receipts, RAG, and Reboots: Legal Tech’s 2025 Year-End Scorecard with Niki Black and Sarah Glassmeyer
author: Niki Black · Sarah Glassmeyer

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s selective-deployment thesis and materially extends it with concrete workflow guidance: define use cases and responsible teams, preserve human verification, avoid generative AI for initial high-stakes research and brief drafting, and prioritise lower-risk or back-office applications. It also links realised value to integrations and pricing-model redesign rather than tool access alone.

st.an: The source endorses selective, practitioner-led learning through balanced analysis, cross-disciplinary perspectives and contextual professional discussion. st.an: The source supports the proposition that rising AI uptake does not itself produce meaningful access-to-justice gains. st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that AI-driven benefits and disruption require organisational preparation rather than following automatically from improved tools. kp.k: Rapid adoption coexists with use-case confusion
kp.d: Glassmeyer argues that ubiquitous, broadly marketed generative AI overwhelms potential users and does not eliminate conventional implementation needs. She reports lawyers wanting Harvey without knowing what they would use it for. Gebauer similarly argues that marketing AI itself, rather than a defined function, makes practical relevance harder to establish.
qs: And I think we’re like overwhelmed with possibilities still.
And they’re like, we don’t know. don’t have a plan.
But like, they’re like, that’s the thing. It’s like the cool kids get Harvey and we want Harvey.

kp.k: Black reports sharply rising survey adoption
kp.d: Citing the 8AM legal industry report, Black says close to three quarters of surveyed individuals used general-purpose tools in daily legal work, compared with 31% last year and 27% the year before. She reports 46% firm adoption of legal-specific tools, describing the prior-year comparison as 'up 21 % last year.' The sample leaned toward solo, small and midsized firms; no sample size or methodology is supplied. She contrasts this with cloud adoption, which remained around 30% for years from about 2015 and exceeded 50% only with the pandemic.
qs: was close to three quarters of the individuals surveyed were using it in their daily legal work, general purpose tools, compared to 31 % last year and 27 % the year before.
And then when you talk about law firms, we found 46 % of law firms
more solo, small and mid-sized firms versus large.
we’re stuck at about 30 % for cloud computing adoption for years, starting in about 2015. And it wasn’t until the pandemic that pushed us over 50%.

kp.k: Embedded AI and enthusiasm facilitate uptake
kp.d: Black observes progressively deeper AI integration into existing legal software, allowing lawyers to use it within familiar tools, while noting that agentic AI discussion exceeds implementation. Lambert reports an unprecedented level of lawyer enthusiasm during 2025, particularly about automating boring work; this is personal observation rather than a measured adoption or productivity result.
qs: mean, agentic, everyone’s talking about agentic AI, but very few people have implemented it.
So people are just able to use AI in a tool that they’re already using.
But just this excitement level is something that I’ve never ever seen before.

kp.k: General-purpose business tiers challenge specialist vendors
kp.d: Black reports that some small-firm technology experts now consider business versions of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude sufficiently protective for most legal work, except particularly sensitive material. This is reported advice, not a demonstrated security finding. She says her report shows more small and midsized firms investing in general-purpose than legal-specific tools, with affordability a major consideration.
qs: a lot of people, especially in the solo and small firm space that are considered experts in this space are suggesting that the business versions of chat GPT, of Gemini, of Claude, are sufficient for, have sufficient protections for the vast majority of legal work.
Harvey’s not cheap and it’s way above the budgets of most small and solo law firms.
there are more law firms investing in chat GPT and those other general purpose tools compared to legal specific tools, at least more at the midsize and small firm level.

kp.k: Foundation-model providers may enter legal markets directly
kp.d: Glassmeyer predicts greater competition from general technology companies in 2026. Black predicts signs in 2026 and stronger movement by mid to late 2027, particularly among midsized and smaller firms already using those ecosystems. Lambert qualifies this scenario by noting OpenAI's current support for legal vendors. Black's suggestion that foundation models could rival specialist output is a forecast, not a comparative test result.
qs: the specialness of legal tech is not going to be always there anymore
I think 2026 you’re going to start to see signs that will happen, but I predict it’s going to be mid to late 2027 where that may start to
Because these are the tools, the ecosystems are already in, and it’s going to make the most sense for them to use them.

kp.k: Human verification remains a professional obligation
kp.d: Glassmeyer frames verification as a continuation of lawyers' longstanding duty to read and check authorities, not an obligation created by generative AI. She compares reliance on AI with overreliance on KeyCite and Shepard's flags, and recommends using legal research providers with underlying corpora for research so lawyers can inspect cited cases. Her account of a developer calling hallucinations a feature is a reported view she questions.
qs: You shouldn’t have been trusting these tools in the past anyway.
We maybe not realized we were dealing in a world where you had to always verify everything coming from these magic boxes, but we really have had to always do this.

I would stick with a legal research company because word that has like a backup of a corpus that it will do rag on and you can go back and read the cases to make sure everything’s being cited correctly.

kp.k: Legal research is a difficult starting task
kp.d: Glassmeyer argues that research is only one part of lawyers' work and AI's possible applications. Its difficulty arises from unsettled law, the process and skill involved, and concentrated access to legal corpora. She recommends beginning with tasks such as timekeeping narratives rather than treating research as the default entry point.
qs: sometimes the right answer is there no right answer that it’s something that it just hasn’t been settled law yet.
there’s basically like four companies now that have like all the law.
why start at that as your entry point to this tool?

kp.k: Repeated AI cross-checking can introduce new errors
kp.d: Black recounts an unidentified sanctions order involving six tools, including legal-specific products, while explicitly expressing uncertainty about which products were used. She argues that passing text between tools can change wording unnoticed rather than constitute reliable verification. She recommends traditional research and an independently written initial brief, preserving the original when using AI for editing or argument checking. Gebauer raises the cost and client-payment implications of repeated checks.
qs: This person used six different tools, some of which were legal specific.
they used all of them to cross check and triple check.
they’re just doing site checking in one, but then it changes some words and they don’t realize they did it because that’s what these tools do.
but keep your original that you wrote, that you did the research on in the traditional tool, that you drafted on your own so that it doesn’t get all screwed up

kp.k: Improved retrieval reportedly strengthens legal research output
kp.d: Lambert reports substantially better research answers around summer 2025, drawing on personal use, a conversation with Ed Walters and two months of investigation rather than a quantified benchmark. He attributes improvement partly to foundation models and partly to combining contextual vector retrieval with knowledge graphs representing court hierarchy and citation status. He repeatedly qualifies the results as imperfect.
qs: Still not perfect, but a hell of a lot better
it’s also put into the knowledge graph so that it understands the hierarchy of the courts, whether it’s overturned, whether it’s been cited.
So the retrieval. part and the augmentation part has advanced quite a bit in the last six months.

kp.k: Consolidation and integration connect practice with business operations
kp.d: Black interprets Clio's acquisition of vLex through earlier consolidation cycles in server-based software, practice management, cloud products and eDiscovery. She argues that AI creates new possibilities for connecting legal work with business management, citing the announced Aderant–Harvey integration. She predicts both acquisitions and integrations rather than universal migration to a single platform, especially where larger firms want to retain preferred tools.
qs: All these companies pop up, there’s massive consolidation. Then there’s just a few big players.
Just today Aderant announced Harvey integration.
So it’s not just going to be acquisitions, it’s going to be integrations.
I don’t necessarily agree that it’s going to be the single platform that everybody works in.

kp.k: Publisher history warns against concentrated supplier power
kp.d: Glassmeyer draws an analogy with legal publishing's consolidation into Thomson Reuters, Lexis and, to an extent, Wolters Kluwer, which she says deprived librarians of bargaining power. She advocates independent companies interoperating through APIs and data standards. Lambert raises the risk that concentrated suppliers extract more value from customers while degrading products; these are concerns rather than demonstrated outcomes of current AI consolidation.
qs: we had no, no choice, no like real power in the relationship.
Keep your small company and integrate.
Will we learn it in the broader legal tech world? I hope so.

kp.k: Clio–vLex could broaden smaller firms' capabilities
kp.d: Glassmeyer is cautiously optimistic that Clio's existing customers will gain access to sophisticated AI tools previously less accessible to them, noting that Harvey does not currently sell to solos. She distinguishes potential profitability benefits from potential access-to-justice benefits and values these opportunities more than Clio's move into BigLaw. These are anticipated benefits, not measured results.
qs: I think it’s really exciting that the traditional Clio customer base will now have access to these kinds of AI tools, which they may not have been able to get to before because Harveys won’t sell the Solos like at present
either for access to justice purposes or for profitability purposes, they’re really going to be able to benefit from these tools

kp.k: Shadow AI calls for training over surveillance
kp.d: Black argues that personal-device access makes comprehensive monitoring impractical and resource-intensive, preferring proper implementation and attention to vendor changes. Glassmeyer recommends risk education, safe experimentation and open reporting without career-ending consequences. Gebauer adds that approved tools must solve actual workflow problems or users will seek unofficial alternatives. Lambert's discussion of Harvey guardrails is his observation, not proof that vendors can contain all risks.
qs: People are going to use these tools regardless of whether you tell them to or not.
surveilling it is not going to be the solution.
give as much like user training and opportunity and like safe spaces for them to experiment.
make it so it’s not going to be the end of their career, the end of their world, if they do tell you they made a mistake.

kp.k: Public evidence of firm-level returns remains contested
kp.d: Lambert says he has not seen major firms publicly demonstrate the financial returns anticipated for 2025 and interprets this as a lack of payoff. Gebauer offers the alternative that firms may be less willing to share results. Their exchange establishes disagreement over the meaning of limited public disclosure, not evidence that all firms have failed to generate returns.
qs: well, we also have to start showing some return on our investment in 2025. I don’t think that that happened.
unless they’re keeping it quiet, which they might be.
I just feel like it’s been a little more closed about sharing.

kp.k: Hourly billing impedes monetising AI efficiency
kp.d: Black argues that efficiency reduces billable hours and predicts clearer returns as alternative fee arrangements expand. She proposes using AI on historical billing and matter data to design competitive, profitable fees. She acknowledges that the entire firm operating system rests on hourly billing, attributing that qualification to Steve Embry. Lambert adds that general counsel incentives often reward hourly discounts rather than alternative pricing, requiring changes on both sides.
qs: Because right now, any increase in efficiency undercuts billable hours.
provide us with an AFA arrangement that will be both competitive and profitable
The entire system of a law firm is set up on that hourly billing framework, so it’s easier said than done.
it’s not what kind of AFA did you get us, it’s what kind of discount did you get us off the billable rate?

kp.k: Sophisticated buyers may accelerate pricing pressure
kp.d: Black argues that AI-equipped corporate legal departments can perform preparatory work internally and challenge outside counsel's hours. She anticipates similar pressure from insurers, drawing on their established invoice scrutiny. She predicts more pressure in 2026 as boutiques offer AFAs and flat fees that undercut large firms; the numerical hours example is illustrative, not a documented client outcome.
qs: And corporate legal counsel are investing in these tools.
They know that I can do half the work ahead of time and hand it off to them and get it.
they’re going to push back and they’re gonna, I’m not gonna pay for this.
especially when boutique firms that spin off and are able to compete and do AFAs and flat fee arrangements, they’re going to start undercutting the large law firms.

kp.k: Back-office automation may deliver returns first
kp.d: Lambert predicts earlier returns in back-office functions because hourly billing obstructs gains from automating fee-earning work; Glassmeyer agrees. As a cross-industry analogy, Lambert recounts an unnamed transportation company reportedly reducing empty-container routing work from three hours to seconds and increasing revenue by 20% in that area. The example is not evidence of equivalent law-firm results.
qs: I do think the first return on investment is gonna be back office.
they used to take a person three hours to do it. And now the AI can do it in seconds and give an answer.
It can be all automated. the people are cut out of the loop.
Lawyer work tools, ROI not so much anytime soon. Backoffice tools, absolutely, yeah.

kp.k: Fragmented discussion weakens professional knowledge exchange
kp.d: Glassmeyer argues that scattered platforms, algorithmic feeds and short-form hot takes make substantive legal-technology exchange harder, recommending renewed long-form blogging. Black agrees that the earlier shared community is unlikely to return, but describes substantive discussion around her LinkedIn writing and argues that the expanded sector now contains distinct professional communities needing partly overlapping spaces.
qs: We can’t really cover what’s happening in that amount of time and have like real.
substantive discussions that we need to have.
we are losing out as an industry that we don’t have a place to like centrally share ideas.
it’s almost like they all need their own spaces with a little bit of overlap.

kp.k: AI dependencies create speculative financial vulnerability
kp.d: Black predicts an AI-related financial shock in 2026 that could contribute to recession and affect legal technology, explicitly acknowledging uncertainty. Glassmeyer highlights compute costs, chips, data-centre construction and legal vendors' dependence on foundation-model providers. She also predicts smaller vendors exhausting their runway and folding or being absorbed, noting 3,000 current Legal Tech Hub listings. These are scenarios and forecasts, not established failures.
qs: I definitely think it’s some sort of financial bubble related to AI. I don’t know what it’s going to look like.
If OpenAI goes under, what’s that going to be for the Harveys of the world?
I have 3,000 listings currently on the legal tech hub
they’re probably gonna fold or get absorbed in some way.

kp.k: Technology competition and job disruption remain uncertain
kp.d: Lambert speculates that Meta and other companies struggling to keep pace with leading AI providers may be vulnerable. Separately, Gebauer predicts disruption in 2026 and possibly the following year as tools take over basic work, while maintaining that new jobs will emerge and hoping organisations prepare their people. Neither forecast supplies employment data or a legal-specific staffing projection.
qs: I think, is in more trouble than people think it is.
if a big company like Meta can be in trouble, just think of the other ones that are trying to develop their, their own AI systems
I am a strong believer that there will be new jobs and new things for people
hopefully you’re going to see organizations preparing their people for that.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Black reports rapid adoption; Glassmeyer distinguishes enthusiasm and availability from purposeful implementation.
pts.d: Niki Black characterises generative-AI adoption as much faster than cloud adoption, supported by her account of the 8AM legal industry survey. She says progressively deeper integrations let lawyers use AI within existing software, although agentic AI remains little implemented. Sarah Glassmeyer argues that ubiquitous, broadly advertised capabilities overwhelm users and that adoption still requires ordinary use-case and organisational work. Her account of lawyers wanting Harvey without knowing what they would do with it illustrates acquisition driven by fear of missing out rather than a productivity plan.

pts.k: General-purpose platforms may erode specialist legal-tech differentiation, especially below the large-firm market.
pts.d: Glassmeyer predicts that major general-purpose AI providers will increasingly treat lawyers as direct customers. Black similarly anticipates outputs approaching specialist tools and competition strengthened by major providers’ investment, advertising reach, affordability and existing software ecosystems. Black reports a developing view among small-firm experts that business tiers offer adequate confidentiality protections for much legal work; this is a reported professional view, not a demonstrated security finding. She also reports more investment in general-purpose than legal-specific tools among surveyed smaller and midsize firms.

pts.k: AI does not eliminate human verification, and cross-checking output through multiple AI tools can introduce further errors.
pts.d: Glassmeyer argues that lawyers must continue reading and verifying underlying authorities, as they should have done with traditional citators. She recommends corpus-backed legal research products for research and considers general-purpose tools more suitable for other workflows. Black describes an unnamed sanctions incident involving multiple tools and argues that repeated AI cross-checking can alter language unnoticed. For research and briefs, she recommends traditional research and a lawyer-written original, with AI confined to editing or argument checks and comparison against the original. These are augmentation-with-verification claims, not claims that autonomous legal research is safe.

pts.k: AI will drive both consolidation and integrations rather than universal migration to a single legal platform.
pts.d: Black argues that AI enables closer integration of the business and practice of law, with the Clio–vLex acquisition prompting competitive responses. She predicts acquisitions alongside many integrations, because firms will retain preferred practice-management, research and document-management products. She expects the largest ultimate players to be general technology companies rather than legal-tech companies. Glassmeyer favours APIs and data standards as alternatives to acquisition and worries that concentration will weaken customer bargaining power. She nevertheless expects Clio–vLex to broaden smaller firms’ access to advanced AI tools.

pts.k: Shadow AI requires useful sanctioned tools, education and safe reporting rather than reliance on surveillance.
pts.d: Black says lawyers will use AI regardless of restrictions, including on personal devices, and argues that constant surveillance consumes resources better spent on proper implementation and tracking vendor changes. Glassmeyer recommends training, safe experimentation and open communication so users understand risks and disclose mistakes rather than conceal them.

pts.k: Black links financial returns to alternative fees and buyer pressure; Glassmeyer expects nearer-term returns in the back office.
pts.d: Black argues that efficiency undercuts revenue under hourly billing and that greater use of alternative fee arrangements will allow firms to capture AI returns. She predicts AI analysis of historical billing and matter data will support competitive, profitable fee proposals. She also says sophisticated corporate buyers are already using AI to do work before instructing firms and will challenge excessive billed time; insurers and fixed-fee boutiques will add pressure. Glassmeyer separately endorses back-office tools as a nearer-term source of return and does not expect comparable returns from lawyer-work tools soon. The transcript supplies no measured legal-firm ROI result.

pts.k: The guests predict financial instability and supplier exits, with legal tech exposed to foundation-model providers.
pts.d: Black predicts a possible AI-related financial bubble and wider recession affecting legal tech, explicitly presenting this as a nonspecific foreboding rather than a substantiated forecast. Glassmeyer identifies dependence on foundation-model companies as a systemic vulnerability. She also predicts that some small legal-tech companies created amid lower entry barriers will exhaust their funding runway and close or be absorbed.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Adoption claims draw on a survey; most other claims rest on experience, anecdotes, market events, analogy or explicit speculation.
pts.d: Black cites the 8AM legal industry report, which she authors, reporting nearly three-quarters of surveyed individuals using general-purpose AI in daily legal work versus 31% and 27% in preceding comparisons, and 46% firm adoption. Her wording around the firm-level 21% comparison is ambiguous about whether it denotes the prior level or an increase. The sample skews toward solo, small and midsize firms; no sample size, sampling method or uncertainty estimates are supplied. Other support includes Black’s long-term tracking of cloud adoption, Glassmeyer’s conversations with tool buyers and founders, Black’s unnamed sanctions order, the Clio–vLex acquisition and Aderant–Harvey integration, historical consolidation in publishing and legal software, and Black’s insurance-litigation experience. Glassmeyer mentions an older citator study, not a generative-AI benchmark. Her financial-risk discussion draws partly on Ed Zitron’s newsletter, without reproducing its calculations. Her 3,000 Legal Technology Hub listings describe the broader directory, not 3,000 AI vendors. No measured hallucination-rate comparison or legal-firm productivity benchmark is provided.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The retrospective concerns 2025; predictions concentrate on 2026, with stronger general-platform displacement expected in mid-to-late 2027.
pts.d: Black describes adoption as accelerating within roughly three years of generative AI’s late-2022 introduction. Glassmeyer frames declining legal-tech distinctiveness as a 2026 prediction. Black expects signs of direct general-platform competition in 2026 and more pronounced effects in mid-to-late 2027, especially in midsize and smaller firms rather than necessarily large firms. Business-tier suitability is qualified by protections, data sensitivity and firm policy; Glassmeyer retains a preference for specialist corpus-backed tools for legal research. Black expects more buyer pressure and alternative-fee competition in 2026, but makes ROI conditional on moving beyond hourly incentives and acknowledges the difficulty of changing the whole firm system. Glassmeyer gives no precise date for back-office ROI beyond contrasting it with lawyer-work returns that are not expected soon. Bubble risks and small-vendor exits are framed around 2026; foundation-provider failure is a conditional scenario, not an asserted event.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Effects differ across smaller firms, large firms, legal-service buyers, individual users and technology suppliers.
pts.d: Solo, small and midsize firms face specialist-tool affordability and availability barriers, making general-purpose business tiers and integrations attractive. Glassmeyer expects Clio’s traditional customers to gain AI capabilities with potential profitability or access-to-justice benefits; she does not demonstrate a reduction in unmet civil legal need. Large firms face pressure on hourly economics and demand for integrations with established systems. Corporate legal departments and insurers are described as sophisticated buyers able to reduce outsourced work and challenge bills, while boutiques may compete through alternative fees. Individual lawyers remain responsible for checking authorities and risk sanctions; staff using unsanctioned tools require education and safe reporting. Specialist vendors face competition from general platforms, consolidation and exposure to upstream providers, while smaller startups may close or be acquired. These claims concern vendors selling tools, not ALSPs delivering legal work.
